content:
Hello, my name is Yoshitsugu Sekine.
I work as a software engineer (web),
and as a hobby I study the mathematical physics of non-relativistic quantum field theory.

I came across the preprint https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.15770,
which is fairly close to my own interests,
and I've been wondering whether I could take on the formalization of the Ising model as a hobby project
-- both as a way to grow as a programmer and in a form that does not get
in the way of those who are seriously pursuing this line of work.

I have professional experience writing Haskell,
but this is my first time seriously working with Lean or any proof assistant,
so I plan to start from the basics.

I am currently recovering from an illness and don't have much time or energy to spare,
so if someone is already working on the formalization of the Ising model,
I will pick a different topic instead (for example, quantum spin systems or the Hubbard model)
so as not to interfere.
If no one has started yet,
I plan to briefly contact the authors of the preprint above before moving forward.

Is anyone currently working on this?
Thanks in advance.
This topic was moved here from #new members > Yoshitsugu Sekine by Kevin Buzzard.
@Yoshitsugu Sekine I've moved your question here because it will get more visibility by the people you want to reach.
@Kevin Buzzard Thank you for your hospitality!

do you mean the continuum limit of the Ising model? I think @Kalle Kytölä is interested in it.

I started to define periodic lattices as subtypes of the continuous torus in this file but I'm very slow at the moment in this project.

More generally @Yoshitsugu Sekine, if you are interested in physics and Lean, we are building an open-source library Physlib (hence the name of this channel), to contain results therefrom. The GitHub is: https://github.com/leanprover-community/physlib.

@Yoh Tanimoto What I currently have in mind is not the continuum limit, but rather phase transitions and critical phenomena of the Ising model.
I'm interested in how inequalities are expressed in a proof assistant, and I'd like to become familiar with the subject through correlation inequalities.
@Joseph Tooby-Smith Thank you! I'll check it.

In particular, I have in mind the discussion in the book by Hara and Tasaki
(https://www.kyoritsu-pub.co.jp/book/b10003637.html, in Japanese).
I took part in the proofreading of this book and my name appears in the preface.
(As a master's student I was at Kawahigashi's group,
one year junior to Tanimoto.)

long time no see!
not sure what you mean by "how inequalities are expressed in a proof assistant" (there are statements like x < y...).
you could try defining the model on a finite lattice (perhaps on ZMod N), the configuration space, the measure and correlation functions.

Honestly, a large part of this is simply that I still lack knowledge of proof assistants.
For example, I can imagine the kind of logical transitions or chains of simple equalities that often appear in introductory material, but I cannot yet picture what it would look like to work out, say, an argument involving sharp constants in an inequality. This is purely my own ignorance, and I will need to study further and search for the right way to articulate it.

If you are interested in the Ising model ( which is an example of a Gibbs Measure ) then this can help https://github.com/YaelDillies/gibbs-measure

Granted we are far from getting Ising model down at the moment

by sharp constant do you mean something like this?

import Mathlib

variable (C : ℝ) (f g : ℝ → ℝ)
#check (∀ x, f x ≤ C * g x) ∧ ∀ C' < C, ∃ x, C' * g x < f x

for the basics of Lean you can start with Mathematics in Lean or The Mechanics of proof
Gibbs measures strike me as a fascinating object in the study of infinite systems. I'm also planning to take a look at the code.
Thank you for the reference page! I'll take a look at that as well. I'm really looking forward to it.

After sleeping on it, I've come to the conclusion that, as far as I can tell, there is currently no Ising model library.
I'm planning to contact the authors of the preprint https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.15770 and then start a repository under the name ising-model.
I have no intention of getting in the way of the experts, so if someone more qualified joins in later and the name or scope ends up conflicting, I'll adjust things accordingly. I'll post here again once the repository is up. Thank you very much.

In case you find it useful to compare or partially build on, there is some exploratory work done in this folder. This was actually a detour from the main goal of the repository (the only one that will likely be developed in the near future) which is mean-field theory.
Thank you for your comment! I'll check that.
